literal: Lord Shi was the eldest son by a concubine of Emperor Zhaocheng.
idiomatic: Lord Shi, born to a concubine, was Emperor Zhaocheng's eldest son.

literal: By nature dull and obstinate, he endured cruelty and lacked benevolence.
idiomatic: He was slow-witted and stubborn, cruel by nature and devoid of mercy.

literal: In the late years of Zhaocheng, Fu Jian sent his Xingtang Duke Fu Luo and others to raid the southern border; Zhaocheng sent Liu Kuren to meet them in battle at Shizi Ridge.
idiomatic: Late in Zhaocheng's reign Fu Jian sent Fu Luo, Duke of Xingtang, and others against the southern marches; Zhaocheng dispatched Liu Kuren to fight them at Shizi Ridge.

literal: At that time Zhaocheng did not prevail and could not personally lead the host in person; he then led the tribes to take refuge in the Yin Mountains and crossed north of the desert.
idiomatic: Zhaocheng was losing and too weak to command the army himself, so he led the tribes into the Yin Mountains and beyond the northern desert.

literal: The Gaoche raided on all sides; he again crossed south of the desert.
idiomatic: Gaoche bands harried them from every quarter, forcing him back south of the desert.

literal: When Fu Luo's army withdrew, he then returned to Yunzhong.
idiomatic: After Fu Luo retreated he returned to Yunzhong.

literal: At first Zhaocheng, because his younger brother Gu yielded the state, gave half the tribes to Gu.
idiomatic: Earlier Zhaocheng had ceded half the realm to his brother Gu when Gu renounced the throne.

literal: When Gu died, his son Jin lost his post and nursed resentment, wishing to watch for an opening to make trouble.
idiomatic: After Gu's death his son Jin, stripped of office, brooded on revenge and waited for a chance to rebel.

literal: At that time Emperor Xianming and Prince Qinming Han had both died first; Taizu was six years old; Zhaocheng was ill; and though Murong the empress's sons Yueba and others were older, the succession was unsettled.
idiomatic: Emperor Xianming and Prince Qinming Han were already dead; Taizu was only six; Zhaocheng lay ill; and though Yueba and other sons of Empress Murong were grown, no heir had been chosen.

literal: Jin thereupon persuaded Lord Shi, saying: "The emperor intends to install the son born of Murong and fears you will make trouble; he wishes to kill you first. That is why in recent days the princes have worn armor, held weapons by night, and circled your lodge waiting for a chance to strike. I pity you and tell you."
idiomatic: Jin then told Lord Shi: "The emperor means to put Murong's son on the throne and, fearing you will rebel, plans to kill you first. That is why the princes have lately gone about in armor at night with weapons in hand, circling your quarters for a chance to strike. Out of pity I warn you."

literal: At that time Fu Luo's army was still at Junzi Ford; by night they were always on alert; the princes wandered among the lodges clutching weapons.
idiomatic: Fu Luo's troops still held Junzi Ford and stood watch through the nights, while the princes paced the lodges armed.

literal: Lord Shi inspected and believed Jin's words; he then led his followers and killed all the princes; Zhaocheng also died suddenly.
idiomatic: Lord Shi looked about, took Jin at his word, and with his men slaughtered every prince; Zhaocheng died the same night.

literal: That night the princes' wives and palace women ran to report to Fu Luo's army; Fu Jian's generals Li Rou and Zhang Hao led troops inward in pressure, and the tribes scattered.
idiomatic: That night the princes' wives and palace women fled to Fu Luo's camp; Fu Jian's generals Li Rou and Zhang Hao pressed inward with troops and the tribes broke apart.

literal: When Fu Jian heard of it he summoned Yan Feng and asked the reason; he answered with the facts.
idiomatic: Fu Jian, hearing the news, summoned Yan Feng and asked what had happened; Yan Feng told him the whole affair.

literal: Fu Jian said: "Evil under heaven is one."
idiomatic: Fu Jian said, "There is only one kind of evil in the world."

literal: He then seized Lord Shi and Jin and had them torn apart at the West Market of Chang'an.
idiomatic: He seized Lord Shi and Jin and had them dismembered at Chang'an's West Market.

literal: Lord Shi's grandson Wuqi held the post of Inspector of Dingzhou and was granted the title Marquis of Linlu.
idiomatic: Lord Shi's grandson Wuqi served as Inspector of Dingzhou and was enfeoffed Marquis of Linlu.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He passed away.

literal: His son Liuzhuang was Marquis of Zhending.
idiomatic: His son Liuzhuang held the title Marquis of Zhending.

literal: His son Yi was seven feet five inches tall, of very imposing appearance, with a fine beard; he had stratagems; in youth he could dance with the sword; in mounted archery he had no peer.
idiomatic: His son Yi stood seven feet five, strikingly handsome with a splendid beard; clever in counsel, he danced with the sword as a youth and was unmatched in mounted archery.

literal: When Taizu visited the Helan tribe, Yi attended him in and out.
idiomatic: When Taizu visited the Helan, Yi attended him wherever he went.

literal: At the beginning of Dengguo he was granted the title Duke of Jiuyuan.
idiomatic: At the opening of the Dengguo era he was made Duke of Jiuyuan.

literal: He followed in breaking the tribes and had merit in planning and battle.
idiomatic: He campaigned in the subjugation of the tribes and won distinction both in counsel and in the field.

literal: When Taizu was about to scheme against Murong Chui, he sent Yi to probe for an opening.
idiomatic: As Taizu prepared to move against Murong Chui he sent Yi to test the enemy.

literal: Chui asked Yi the meaning of Taizu not coming in person; Yi said: "From our forebears down, we have held the northern lands generation after generation, and our descendants have succeeded without losing the old order.
idiomatic: Chui asked why Taizu had not come himself; Yi replied: "Since our ancestors' time we have held the north, generation after generation, without forfeiting our heritage.

literal: Our founding ancestor received the Jin calendar,[3] was enfeoffed as King of Dai, and eastward we and Yan have been brothers for generations.
idiomatic: Our founder accepted investiture under the Jin calendar,[3] took the title King of Dai, and for generations Yan and we have stood as brothers in the east.

literal: That Yi should come on command is, by reason, no fault."
idiomatic: My coming on orders is, by rights, no lapse."

literal: Chui admired his reply and jested, saying: "My might fills the four seas; your lord will not come to see me—how is that not a fault?"
idiomatic: Chui admired the answer and said in jest, "My power spans the seas—yet your master will not come to see me. How is that no fault?"

literal: Yi said: "If Yan will not cultivate civil virtue and wishes to strengthen itself by military might, that is the business of our commanders; it is not for Yi to know."
idiomatic: Yi said, "If Yan neglects civil virtue and trusts only to arms, that is a matter for our generals, not for me to judge."

literal: When he returned he reported: "Chui may be taken only when he is dying; not yet."
idiomatic: On his return he reported, "Chui can be struck only when he is near death—not yet."

literal: Taizu changed color and questioned him.
idiomatic: Taizu's face darkened and he pressed him for an explanation.

literal: Yi said: "Chui is already old; his son Bao is weak and without authority; in counsel he cannot decide.
idiomatic: Yi said, "Chui is old; his son Bao is feeble and commands no awe; he cannot settle on a plan.

literal: Murong De trusts in his own talent and is no minister for a weak master.
idiomatic: Murong De is proud of his gifts and will not serve a feeble lord.

literal: A breach will rise within; he may be taken by design."
idiomatic: Strife will break out within their house—then they can be taken."

literal: Taizu thought it so.
idiomatic: Taizu agreed.

literal: Later his enfeoffment was changed to Duke of Pingyuan.
idiomatic: He was later reassigned as Duke of Pingyuan.

literal: When Taizu campaigned against Wei Chen, Yi marched by a separate route, obtained Wei Chen's corpse, and sent the head to the traveling palace.
idiomatic: On Taizu's campaign against Wei Chen, Yi took a separate road, seized Wei Chen's body, and sent the head to the field headquarters.

literal: Taizu was greatly pleased and transferred his enfeoffment to Duke of Dongping.
idiomatic: Taizu was delighted and raised him to Duke of Dongping.

literal: He was ordered to supervise garrison farming in Hebei, from Wuyuan to beyond Yusang Pass, dividing the crops; he won great popular regard.
idiomatic: He was ordered to oversee garrison agriculture in Hebei from Wuyuan to beyond Yusang Pass, apportioning the harvests, and won deep loyalty among the people.

literal: When Murong Bao raided Wuyuan, Yi held Shuofang in his stead and blocked Bao's line of retreat.
idiomatic: When Murong Bao struck at Wuyuan, Yi held Shuofang and barred his retreat.

literal: When Bingzhou was pacified, Yi's merit was great and he was promoted to Director of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: After Bingzhou was pacified his service stood foremost and he was made Director of the Masters of Writing.

literal: He followed in the siege of Zhongshan.
idiomatic: He took part in the siege of Zhongshan.

literal: When Murong De was defeated, Taizu gave Yi Murong Pulong's wife Lady Zhou, together with her servants and goods.
idiomatic: After Murong De's defeat Taizu gave Yi Lady Zhou, Murong Pulong's wife, with her household and possessions.

literal: Soon he was moved to Grand Commander of All Armies Within and Without and Left Chancellor, and advanced to Prince of Wei.
idiomatic: He was soon made Grand Commander of All Armies Within and Without and Left Chancellor, and was raised to Prince of Wei.

literal: When Zhongshan was pacified, Yi was again sent to attack Ye and pacified it.
idiomatic: After Zhongshan fell he was sent again to take Ye and subdued it.

literal: When Taizu was about to return to the Dai capital, he set up a traveling secretariat at Zhongshan, ordered Yi to remain Director of the Masters of Writing to guard it, and near and far submitted in trust.
idiomatic: As Taizu prepared to return to the Dai capital he established a traveling secretariat at Zhongshan and left Yi as Director of the Masters of Writing to hold the city; the region submitted willingly.

literal: Soon Yi was summoned to enter court as chancellor to assist.
idiomatic: Yi was soon recalled to serve at court as chancellor.

literal: He again followed on the campaign against the Gaoche.
idiomatic: He campaigned again against the Gaoche.

literal: Yi separately marched from the northwest and broke their detached division.
idiomatic: Yi took a separate route from the northwest and shattered a detached Gaoche force.

literal: He again followed in attacking Yao Ping and had merit; he was granted silk, cloth, cotton, cattle, horses, sheep, and the like.
idiomatic: He joined the attack on Yao Ping and was rewarded with silk, cloth, cotton, cattle, horses, sheep, and the like.

literal: Yi's bodily strength surpassed others; his bow drew nearly ten stone;
idiomatic: Yi's strength was extraordinary; his bow drew nearly ten stone;

literal: Duke of Chenliu Qian's spear was greatly praised as exceptional.
idiomatic: and Duke of Chenliu Qian's spear was famed as matchless.

literal: People of the time said: "Prince of Wei's bow, Prince Huan's spear."
idiomatic: Men said at the time, "Prince of Wei's bow, Prince Huan's spear."

literal: When Shizu was first born, Taizu rejoiced and summoned Yi at night.
idiomatic: When Shizu was born Taizu rejoiced and called Yi to him at night.

literal: Taizu said: "When you heard a night summons, were you not startled and afraid?"
idiomatic: Taizu asked, "When you were summoned at night, were you not afraid?"

literal: Yi said: "Your servant serves Your Majesty with full loyalty; Your Majesty is discerning, and your servant is always at ease.
idiomatic: Yi said, "I serve Your Majesty with open heart; Your Majesty sees clearly, and I am always at peace.

literal: Suddenly to receive a night edict—wonder there may be, but fear there is none."
idiomatic: A sudden summons at night may surprise, but it never frightens me."

literal: Taizu told him of Shizu's birth; Yi rose, bowed, and sang and danced; they then drank facing each other until dawn.
idiomatic: Taizu told him of Shizu's birth; Yi rose, bowed, sang and danced for joy, and they drank together until dawn.

literal: He summoned the ministers to enter and granted Yi the imperial horse, imperial belt, silks, and brocades.
idiomatic: He then summoned the court and gave Yi the imperial horse, belt, silks, and brocades.

literal: Earlier, Hou Ji of Shanggu, Zhang Gun, Xu Qian of Dai commandery, and others were famed in their time, learned in past and present; when they first entered the state they heard Yi treated scholars well and went first to Yi.
idiomatic: Earlier Hou Ji of Shanggu, Zhang Gun, Xu Qian of Dai, and other scholars famed for learning had come into the realm; hearing Yi honored talent, they sought him out first.

literal: Yi received them all with ceremony; together they discussed affairs of the age, traced rivers and mountains, distinguished cities and towns, and success and failure at key points—offhand he could set them all forth.
idiomatic: Yi welcomed them all and debated the affairs of the day, mapping rivers and passes, naming cities and strongpoints, and weighing victory and defeat at every hinge—he could rehearse them all without pause.

literal: Qian and the others sighed in admiration and said to one another: "The Duke of Pingyuan has great talent and a strategy not of this age; we should attach ourselves to his train."
idiomatic: Qian and the rest marveled and said to one another, "The Duke of Pingyuan has genius and a strategy for the ages—we should follow in his wake."

literal: Because of Yi's capacity and reputation Taizu treated him with especial weight, often visiting his residence with the courtesy due family.
idiomatic: Taizu valued Yi's stature and often visited his house with the ease of kin.

literal: Yi, proud of his merit and trusting in favor, then joined Duke of Yidu Mu Chong in plotting rebellion, hid armed men to wait for Taizu, and intended treason.
idiomatic: Proud of his deeds and secure in Taizu's favor, Yi conspired with Duke of Yidu Mu Chong, posted swordsmen to ambush Taizu, and planned treason.

literal: Chong's son Suiliu remained among the hidden swordsmen; Taizu summoned him, about to give him a mission.
idiomatic: Chong's son Suiliu was among the hidden men when Taizu called for him on other business.

literal: Suiliu heard the summons, feared exposure, climbed the wall to report the plot, and Taizu kept it secret and pardoned him.
idiomatic: Hearing the summons Suiliu feared discovery, scaled the wall to reveal the plot, and Taizu concealed the matter and spared him.

literal: In the sixth year of Tiansi many heavenly signs changed; diviners said, "There will be a rebellious minister; corpses will lie and blood will flow."
idiomatic: In the sixth year of Tiansi the heavens showed many omens; diviners said a traitor would die amid slaughter.

literal: Taizu hated this and killed many ministers and dukes, wishing to appease the disaster.
idiomatic: Taizu loathed the omen and executed many high officials, hoping to turn aside the calamity.

literal: Yi was uneasy within and fled alone on horseback.
idiomatic: Yi, shaken within, fled alone on horseback.

literal: Taizu sent men in pursuit to seize him and then granted him death; he was buried with commoner's rites.
idiomatic: Taizu had him pursued, seized, and granted death; he was buried with common rites.

literal: Yi had fifteen sons.
idiomatic: Yi left fifteen sons.

literal: His son Zuan, five years old, Taizu ordered reared in the palace.
idiomatic: His son Zuan, aged five, Taizu ordered raised in the palace.

literal: From youth he was bright and keen; in movement and rest he observed propriety; Taizu loved him and his favor matched the other princes.
idiomatic: Clever and courteous from childhood, he won Taizu's love equal to the imperial sons.

literal: When Shizu ascended the throne he was appointed Inspector of Dingzhou, enfeoffed Duke of Zhongshan, advanced to prince, and granted a hand-drawn carriage and folding stool as special honors.
idiomatic: At Shizu's accession he became Inspector of Dingzhou, was made Duke of Zhongshan and then prince, and received a hand-drawn carriage and folding stool as marks of favor.

literal: [4] Zuan loved wine and favored flatterers; government was accomplished by bribes; Shizu killed his close favorites.
idiomatic: [4] Zuan drank heavily and kept sycophants; office went to the highest bidder until Shizu executed his pet courtiers.

literal: Later he repented, cultivated caution, and was appointed Grand General of the Inner Palace.
idiomatic: He later repented, grew careful in conduct, and was made Grand General of the Inner Palace.

literal: In office he was clear, sparing, and simple in caution; opinion again praised him as honest and fair.
idiomatic: In office he lived plainly and carefully, and men again praised his integrity.

literal: Zuan was eldest among the clan kindred; when the imperial house had affairs, all came to consult him.
idiomatic: As the senior of the clan, he was the one the imperial kindred consulted in every family matter.

literal: He died; posthumous title Jian.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously styled Jian.

literal: Zuan's younger brother Liang was loyal and sincere by nature.
idiomatic: Zuan's brother Liang was steadfast and true by nature.

literal: Emperor Taizong, recalling Yi's merit, enfeoffed Liang Prince of Nanyang to continue Yi's line.
idiomatic: Emperor Taizong, recording Yi's service, made Liang Prince of Nanyang to carry on his line.

literal: His son Zhen understood the languages of many regions and was skilled in riding and archery.
idiomatic: His son Zhen mastered many tongues and excelled in horsemanship and archery.

literal: In Shizu's time he was Director of the Palace Guards.
idiomatic: Under Shizu he served as Director of the Palace Guards.

literal: He followed on the campaign against the Rouran; suddenly they met a detached band of the enemy; they were fewer and could not match them; Zhen then went to a hill, removed saddle and let horses graze, to show there were ambush troops; the enemy indeed suspected and avoided them.
idiomatic: On campaign against the Rouran he suddenly met a detached band too numerous to fight; Zhen rode to a hill, slipped saddles, and loosed the horses as if an ambush lay hidden—the enemy suspected a trap and withdrew.

literal: At the beginning of Gaozu he was granted the title Duke of Pei commandery.
idiomatic: Early in Gaozu's reign he was made Duke of Pei.

literal: Later he was appointed Inspector of Southern Yuzhou.
idiomatic: He was later appointed Inspector of Southern Yuzhou.

literal: The barbarians of Great Hu Mountain raided from time to time; former governors and protectors for the most part only held them loosely in check.
idiomatic: The tribes of Great Hu Mountain raided often, and earlier governors had done little more than placate them.

literal: Zhen then laid a plan, summoned more than thirty chieftains of the Xincai and Xiangcheng barbarians, arrayed himself in full martial dress west of the prefecture, set out wine for them, and had them watch archery.
idiomatic: Zhen devised a stratagem: he summoned more than thirty chiefs of the Xincai and Xiangcheng tribes, appeared west of the city in full armor, feasted them, and made them watch an archery display.

literal: First he chose more than twenty skilled archers from his attendants; Zhen himself shot several arrows and all hit; then he ordered the attendants to shoot in turn, and all hit.
idiomatic: He first chose twenty-odd expert bowmen from his guard; Zhen shot several arrows himself, every one on target, then had his men shoot in turn—all hit.

literal: First he brought out a condemned prisoner and had him wear military dress and take part in the shooting as well; he ordered that if he did not hit, Zhen would rebuke and behead him.
idiomatic: He then produced a condemned man in soldier's dress to shoot with the rest, with orders that Zhen would rebuke and behead him on a miss.

literal: The barbarian chieftains and others submitted in awe of his martial power, looked at one another, and their thighs trembled.
idiomatic: The chieftains cowered before his show of force, glancing at one another with shaking knees.

literal: He also beforehand instructed his attendants to take ten condemned men, all dress them in barbarian clothes, and say they were raiding bandits.
idiomatic: He had also secretly prepared ten condemned men dressed as raiders and passed off as bandits.

literal: Zhen then sat in audience, feigned to lift his eyes to heaven; there was a slight stir of wind; Zhen said to the barbarians: "The wind is somewhat violent; it seems raiding bandits have entered the border—not more than ten men, and they should be about fifty li to the southwest."
idiomatic: Zhen then took his seat, pretended to scan the sky, and when a breeze stirred said to the tribesmen, "The wind runs fierce—raiders have crossed the border, no more than ten, about fifty li southwest."

literal: He at once ordered horsemen to pursue and seize them; indeed they bound and sent ten men.
idiomatic: He sent horsemen at once; they returned with exactly ten bound men.

literal: Zhen told the barbarians: "When men of your villages act as bandits like this, do they deserve death or not?"
idiomatic: Zhen asked the chiefs, "When your people raid like this, do they deserve death?"

literal: The barbarians all knocked their heads and said: "They deserve ten thousand deaths."
idiomatic: They kowtowed and cried, "They deserve death a thousand times over."

literal: Zhen then beheaded them.
idiomatic: Zhen had the ten men beheaded on the spot.

literal: He then sent the barbarians back and also added words of comfort and instruction.
idiomatic: He sent the chiefs home with soothing words.

literal: The barbarians were greatly subdued; from then on within the borders there was no violent plunder; more than three thousand households of people south of the Huai came in succession to submit; they were placed on the east bank of the Ru River within the city and called the Ward of Returning Allegiance.
idiomatic: The tribes were thoroughly cowed; raiding ceased within his borders, and more than three thousand households south of the Huai came over; he settled them east of the city along the Ru in a quarter named Returning Allegiance.

literal: At first the magnate of Yuzhou city Hu Qiusheng had several times communicated with outsiders.
idiomatic: Earlier the city magnate Hu Qiusheng of Yuzhou had repeatedly dealt with outsiders.
